                                         1    Introduction

                                         Agentic evaluation is increasingly centered on long-horizon, interactive tasks. Benchmarks such as SWE-
                                         bench [Jimenez et al., 2024], DeepSWE [Huang et al., 2026], and Terminal-Bench [Merrill et al., 2026] evaluate
                                         sustained software-engineering and terminal interaction, while challenging knowledge-oriented benchmarks
                                         such as Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE) [Phan et al., 2025] continue to raise the capability frontier. Yet these
                                         evaluations are used almost exclusively after post-training.

                                         During pretraining, however, there remains no established way to evaluate how base models behave on
                                         end-to-end agentic tasks. Such an evaluation could help track changes across pretraining checkpoints,
                                         characterize differences between training stages, and expose behavioral deficiencies that are difficult to
                                         observe through conventional static benchmarks alone.

                                         The main challenge is that existing agent benchmarks assume instruction-following models: their scaffolds
                                         rely on system prompts, chat templates, prescribed tool formats, and stable multi-turn interaction. Pretrained
                                         base models are not explicitly trained for these protocols, and directly inserting them into standard agent
                                         scaffolds often produces malformed or unstable trajectories. One alternative is to fine-tune each checkpoint
                                         before evaluation, but repeated SFT introduces additional cost and changes the model being evaluated.
                                         As a result, existing pretraining-side evaluations largely rely on static or likelihood-based proxies, such as

trajectory-derived QA tasks [Qin et al., 2025] or code and trajectory likelihood [Cursor Research et al., 2026,
DeepSeek-AI, 2026]. These signals are useful for model comparison, but provide limited visibility into how
the evaluated model itself interacts with an environment.

This distinction matters because scalar proxy scores cannot show whether a model explores the environment,
makes useful edits, tests its hypotheses, revises after failed attempts, or simply fails to make progress.
End-to-end interaction therefore provides a complementary view: in addition to final task success, it exposes
the execution process through which that outcome is reached. This leads to the central question of our work:

    Can we evaluate pretrained base models on end-to-end agentic tasks without first turning them into
                                     instruction-following models?

We introduce ASAP (Agent Scaffold Adaptation for Pretraining Evaluation), a lightweight framework for
adapting existing agent scaffolds to pretrained base models. Our key principle is that base models should
be evaluated as continuation models rather than incomplete chat models. ASAP preserves the completion
interface and modifies only the model-facing interaction protocol through three simple components: a
Markdown+XML trajectory format, a short reference trajectory prefix, and minimal recovery from structural
failures such as premature submission or repeated actions.

Across software-engineering and deep-research settings, ASAP yields discriminative end-to-end performance
across base models and remains sensitive to differences between checkpoints within the same pretraining run.
In our pretraining-stage study, ASAP continues to separate checkpoints even when conventional pretraining
benchmarks change only marginally. More importantly, the resulting execution trajectories make it possible
to characterize these differences in behavioral terms, including changes in exploration, editing, testing,
recovery, and task completion. Comparing base and post-trained models further illustrates how execution
patterns differ after post-training.

These results suggest that end-to-end agent evaluation can complement conventional pretraining benchmarks
by providing a practical behavioral diagnostic of model behaviors.

Our contributions are:

• End-to-end evaluation of pretrained base models. We introduce ASAP, a lightweight adaptation of
  existing agent scaffolds that enables pretrained base models to execute agentic tasks through their native
  completion interface, without weight updates.
• A sensitive probe of agent-relevant behavior during pretraining. ASAP distinguishes both different base
  models and checkpoints within the same training run, including stages where conventional pretraining
  benchmarks show only small changes.
• Trajectory-level diagnosis of behavioral change. ASAP exposes model-generated execution trajectories,
  enabling fine-grained analysis of how exploration, editing, testing, recovery, and task completion vary
  across pretraining checkpoints and after post-training.

3         Methodology

We evaluate a pretrained base model directly through a simple text completions task, treating agent execution
as a continuation problem rather than converting the model into a chat-style interface. In particular, we do
not apply a chat template or system prompt. Instead, we adapt the underlying agent scaffold with a small
set of simple design principles that make base-model generation sufficiently stable for end-to-end agent
evaluation. ASAP is built around three components: (1) representing each interaction step in a structured
Markdown+XML trajectory format, (2) bootstrapping the model with a short reference prefix that serves as
in-context guidance for how to continue the trajectory, and (3) lightweight recovery from structural failures
such as repeated actions and empty submit to prevent degenerate loops. Figure 1 provides an overview of
the complete ASAP evaluation pipeline.



3.1            Markdown and XML Shell-Log Format

We formulate agent interaction as a structured text continuation task rather than a conversational one. Each
step uses Markdown for free-form thinking and XML tags (e.g., <bash> and <observation>) to delimit


                                                                                                                3
                                                                                                         ASAP


actions and environment feedback. This representation resembles structured text and shell-log patterns
commonly seen during pretraining, making it natural for base models to continue. Among alternative
formats including pure JSON, XML, and Markdown, the hybrid Markdown+XML format yields the most
stable trajectories in our experiments (Appendix A.4.1). An illustrative format example is provided in
Appendix A.2.



Thought-action generation. At each agent step, a single completion call generates both the model’s
thinking and its subsequent action. Generation starts from ## Thinking and stops after a complete action
(e.g., </bash> or a terminal action). The harness executes the action, appends the resulting output as an
<observation> block, and continues the trajectory. Execution terminates upon <submit/>, the maximum
number of steps, or detection of a degenerate repeated-action loop.



3.2   Reference Trajectory Prefix Bootstrapping

Unlike instruction-tuned models, pretrained base models are not explicitly trained to initiate a prescribed
agent workflow from a standalone task instruction. We therefore prepend a short segment from a reference
agent trajectory, turning the evaluation into continuation of an already established interaction process. The
prefix plays a role similar to few-shot context in conventional base-model evaluation: it helps the model enter
the intended interaction pattern and provides lightweight task navigation, while leaving the substantive
task solving to the evaluated model.

For each instance, we take the initial steps from a reference trajectory produced by an instruction-tuned
model and use them as the bootstrap prefix. These steps may provide limited task-relevant guidance,
such as exposing the repository structure or inspecting potentially relevant files, but we verify that they
do not directly reveal the solution or contain the target patch. The remaining trajectory is then generated
autonomously by the evaluated base model. For each instance, the same prefix is used across all evaluated
models, providing a controlled basis for comparison across models and pretraining checkpoints.

Additional details on prefix construction, length ablations, and robustness to reference-source resampling
are provided in Appendix A.4.2.



3.3   Lightweight Recovery from Structural Failures

Even with trajectory-format guidance and reference-prefix bootstrapping, base models can occasionally fall
into structural failure modes from which they do not recover autonomously. We observe two recurring
patterns during harness development: premature submission before making any effective edit, and repeated
execution of the same action. We apply a lightweight intervention to each case, providing the model with a
single opportunity to recover before terminating the trajectory.



Premature submission recovery. Some base models exhibit a submit bias, emitting <submit/> before
modifying any source file. On the first such attempt, we reject the submission and append a short hint
indicating that at least one source file should be edited before submission. The model is then allowed to
continue autonomously. If it again attempts to submit without producing an effective edit, we accept the
submission as an empty patch and terminate the trajectory.

Repeated-action recovery. Another common failure mode is repeated actions, in which the model issues
the same action without making progress. When such repetition is first detected, we suppress the redundant
action and append a short hint asking the model to try a different approach. If the model subsequently falls
into the same repeated-action pattern again, we terminate the trajectory.

These interventions are deliberately minimal: each failure mode triggers at most one textual hint, and the
harness never inserts task-specific actions or edits on behalf of the model. If the base model cannot recover

5       Extensive Analysis

In this section, we use ASAP to study how agentic capabilities evolve across pretraining and how they are
subsequently affected by post-training. We first analyze capability changes across pretraining stages and
decompose them into specific behavioral transitions in Section 5.1, and then examine the changes from
base to post-trained models in Section 5.2. We further find that the model ordering exposed by ASAP is
preserved after applying the same lightweight SFT recipe, and the potential evaluation hacking through
external network access is scarce for base models. These details can be found in Appendix A.5 and A.6.



5.1     Monitoring Pretraining Progress and Behavioral Transitions

We evaluate checkpoints from different pretraining stages of our self-trained 30B-A3B MoE base model M
with ASAP. By using ASAP we could examine how agentic capability evolves over the course of pretraining.
Specifically, we study whether ASAP can sensitively distinguish checkpoints at different stages of pretrain-
ing, and, beyond aggregate performance gains, identify which agentic behaviors improve as pretraining
progresses. The latter analysis is enabled by the execution trajectories collected through our end-to-end
evaluation: rather than observing only changes in final scores, we can decompose these gains into changes
in specific agent behaviors. This demonstrates that ASAP serves not only as a discriminative benchmark for
pretraining checkpoints, but also as a diagnostic tool for understanding how agentic capabilities emerge and
evolve during pretraining.



Experimental setup. We evaluate nine checkpoints spanning five stages with ASAP on SWE-bench Verified.
Mid-stage checkpoints are included to measure within-stage progress (stagex-mid means 23 training tokens
of stage x). Stage1 is general pretraining; stage2 applies learning-rate decay over a higher-quality mixture
with QA and instruction-following data but no agentic trajectories; stage3 first introduces trajectory-like data
together with 32K long-context training; and stages 4 and 5 continue trajectory training while extending the
training context to 128K and 256K, respectively. For comparison, we use the aggregate of our conventional
pretraining evaluations , which cover knowledge & factual QA, mathematics, reasoning and code.



5.1.1    Cross-stage performance on ASAP and general benchmarks


Figure 2(a) shows how performance on ASAP evolves across pretraining stages. The largest transition occurs
from stage2 to stage3, where trajectory-like data is introduced together with native 32K long-context training.
   MMLU (-pro,-redux), SimpleQA, INCLUDE, GPQA, GSM8K, MGSM, BBH, MATH500, EvalPlus, Livecodebench, CruxEval,
across the corpus, resulting in substantial data construction costs (Wei et al., 2026b). Training memory
modules on these targets further incurs significant computational cost. Moreover, these methods
rely on shallow fusion through output-probability interpolation, without incorporating memory into
the decoder’s hidden states. Intuitively, integrating memory into intermediate hidden states allows
subsequent layers to further process and combine it with the evolving context. The broader challenge
is to enable language models to acquire external knowledge efficiently and use it effectively.
In this work, we introduce Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), a parametric memory architecture that
combines efficient knowledge acquisition with deep fusion within the decoder (Figure 1). At a high
level, DFM shares memory supervision across multiple token predictions while allowing each token to
use the learned memory according to its context. We jointly train a memory predictor and a memory
fusion module, using retrieved target memory to supervise the predictor and the standard language
modeling objective to train both modules. In this way, external knowledge is not only stored in the
predictor’s parameters, but also injected into intermediate hidden states through the fusion module,
allowing subsequent decoder layers to utilize the memory during generation. The LLM backbone
remains frozen throughout, and memory prediction is performed at the chunk level.
Our experiments demonstrate improvements in both efficiency and downstream performance. Com-
pared with existing parametric memory approaches that construct token-level memory targets, DFM
requires 32× fewer retrieval queries and 2048× fewer retrieved items to construct its training data.
DFM achieves the highest average score across six QA tasks on both backbones, outperforming
the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA,
adaptation across code, mathematics, and law yields average gains of 6.51 and 4.38 points over
Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively. Ablations further highlight the importance of
fusion placement and gate initialization, while showing comparatively small changes in average QA
performance across the tested chunk sizes and numbers of memory slots.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
• We introduce DFM, a parametric memory architecture with deep fusion, which integrates
  learned corpus knowledge into intermediate hidden states so that subsequent decoder layers can
  process memory together with the evolving context. Inference requires no explicit retrieval.
• We reduce the overhead of supervision construction and memory training through chunk-level
  supervision and end-to-end training with a frozen backbone. For training data construction, DFM
  requires 32× fewer retrieval queries and 2048× fewer retrieved items than existing parametric
  memory approaches based on token-level targets.
• We demonstrate improved QA performance and domain adaptation. Across six QA tasks, DFM
  performs better over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-
  Base. Across code, mathematics, and law, average gains over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base
  reach 6.51 and 4.38 points, respectively.


2. Related Work
Model Adaptation. Continued pretraining adapts language models to additional corpora through
further language modeling (Gururangan et al., 2020), while LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) offers a parameter-
efficient way to adapt the model. Such adaptation can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously
acquired capabilities (Biderman et al., 2024). Deep Fusion Memory keeps the backbone frozen and


                                                                                                       2
                                       Deep Fusion Memory

learns an added memory module from retrieval-derived targets, jointly training memory prediction
and fusion.
Retrieval-Augmented Language Models. Non-parametric memory exposes corpus information
through several interfaces. 𝑘NN-LM retrieves context–token pairs and interpolates a neighbor-derived
next-token distribution with the language model output (Khandelwal et al., 2019), whereas RAG
conditions generation on retrieved passages (Lewis et al., 2020). RETRO combines chunk retrieval
with cross-attention inside the Transformer (Borgeaud et al., 2022). xRAG projects a retrieved
document embedding into a single token representation prepended to the query, reducing the context
passed to the generator (Cheng et al., 2024). These methods retain an external retrieval dependency
at inference. Deep Fusion Memory predicts continuous memory parametrically and uses it inside the
decoder without online search.
Parametric Memory. MLP Memory trains an MLP to predict 𝑘NN token distributions from language
model representations (Wei et al., 2026a). Memory Decoder learns a similar distributional target
with a standalone decoder (Cao et al., 2026). Memory Decoder at Scale extends this approach to
large-scale general and domain memory pretraining (Wei et al., 2026b). MemSFT specializes frozen
backbones through a domain memory and a learned token-wise router over the backbone and memory
output distributions (Wang et al., 2026). These approaches avoid explicit retrieval at inference, but
token-level retrieval incurs substantial data construction costs, and output-probability interpolation
provides only shallow fusion. Deep Fusion Memory reduces the cost of supervision construction by
sharing target memory across tokens within each chunk and fuses predicted memory into hidden
states through gated cross-attention.


3. Deep Fusion Memory
Deep Fusion Memory consists of a causal chunk-level memory predictor and memory cross-attention
modules inserted into selected decoder layers (Figure 1). We construct target memory offline, then
jointly train the added modules with language-modeling and memory-prediction objectives while
keeping the backbone frozen. At inference, the predictor supplies memory directly from the input
sequence.

The MSE excludes 𝑋0 , which has no preceding chunk. We set 𝛽 = 1. The MSE is computed directly

the predicted memory slots. The predictor, query projection, memory projector, cross-attention, and
gate parameters are optimized jointly. The backbone, retrieval encoder, and target memory remain
fixed.


3.3. Inference

At inference, the language model uses the same predictor and fusion modules without constructing
target memory. Chunk queries are formed from backbone input embeddings, and the memory
predictor supplies predicted memory to the selected decoder layers. No datastore search, retrieved
text, or external embedding encoder is required. For QA evaluation, predicted memory is computed
from the visible prompt and remains fixed during answer generation. Selected decoder layers attend
to the predicted memory only at positions associated with the prompt chunks. As defined in Eq. 2, a
sigmoid gate conditioned on the current token state scales each head before output projection. With
layer-specific gate parameters, the contribution of the fixed memory can vary across tokens, heads,
and layers.


4. Experiments
We evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of DFM across knowledge-intensive question answering
and domain adaptation. We first describe the datasets, training configurations, and baselines (§4.1).


                                                                                                   5
                                      Deep Fusion Memory

We then evaluate DFM on six knowledge-intensive question-answering tasks (§4.2) and examine
its effectiveness beyond QA through domain adaptation in Code, Math, and Law (§4.3). Finally,
we compare parameter overhead, training time, and target-construction workload with token-level
memory (§4.4).


4.1. Experimental Setup

Datasets. For question answering, we train on English Wikipedia from December 2018, comprising
approximately 4B tokens. We evaluate single-hop QA on NQ (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019) and We-
bQA (Berant et al., 2013), and multi-hop QA on HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018), 2WikiMultiHopQA (Ho
et al., 2020), MuSiQue (Trivedi et al., 2022), and Bamboogle (Press et al., 2023). For domain adapta-
tion, we sample subsets from Swallow-Code (Fujii et al., 2026) and Swallow-Math (Fujii et al., 2026),
and use legal text from DISC-Law-SFT (Yue et al., 2023). We evaluate Code on HumanEval (Chen
et al., 2021) and HumanEval+ (Liu et al., 2023), Math on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), and Law on
LawBench (Fei et al., 2024). Appendices A.1 and A.2 give data-construction and evaluation details
for QA and domain adaptation.

                                         1   I NTRODUCTION

                                         Long-context inputs underpin exciting recent language model deployments, where the model’s abil-
                                         ity to process vast swaths of personalized user data and live content during inference has led to
                                         transformative capabilities in deep research, large-scale document processing, coding agents, and
                                         data agents (OpenAI, 2025b; Gemini, 2025; Anthropic, 2025b;a; Anysphere, 2025; GitHub, 2025).
                                         When processing large inputs, like code or long documents, experts readers skim to closely read
                                         only what matters. Yet, transformers process every token of their input through each layer, whether
                                         or not the token bears critical information. The cost of this full read is attention compute that grows
                                         quadratically with input length, as well as MLP compute and KV-cache memory that grow linearly,
                                         making long-context prefill a key bottleneck in model serving.
                                         Recent research proposes to address this efficiency challenge for long-context prefill through two
                                         primary approaches. First, one body of work proposes training-free token pruning, using attention-
                                         based scoring heuristics to prune token hidden states, forwarding only the highest-scoring tokens
                                         to upper layers (Jo et al., 2025; Long et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2024; Yang et al.,
                                         2024a; Fu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2021). These methods are inexpensive to
                                         deploy, requiring no model training, but demonstrate limited speedups before degrading accuracy.
                                         Alternatively, a large body of work instead develops architectural modifications to the standard
                                         transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017). These methods offer promising prefill-efficiency
                                         improvements, but are expensive to train, often requiring pre-training from scratch and substantially
                                         different hardware and software than existing ecosystems (Dehghani et al., 2018; Bae et al., 2025;
                                         Graves, 2016; Raposo et al., 2024; Ainslie et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2021; He et al., 2025; Gu & Dao,

gate module keeps K of them, and every layer above L processes only those K tokens. (b) The gate module
scores each hidden state with a small scoring network, and a top-K selector forwards the kept hidden states
together with their importance scores. (c) Token-gated attention multiplies each attention weight by the gate
value gj of its key, which enables end-to-end training. (d) On 2WikiMultihopQA question answering, with
Qwen3-1.7B, T OKEN G ATE pushes the Pareto frontier of accuracy versus time-to-first-token and peak prefill

2023; Dao & Gu, 2024). To bridge this gap, we ask the question, can we endow existing trained
models with improved long-context prefill efficiency while maintaining strong accuracy?
In this work, we introduce T OKEN G ATE, a small, drop-in component that extends transformer-based
models, enabling end-to-end trainable token pruning over long-context inputs for efficient prefill.
The model forward pass using T OKEN G ATE decomposes into three parts, as Figure 1a shows. First,
layers below the gate module perform a standard forward pass, processing all tokens through each
layer. Second, tokens pass through the gate module, which produces a score for each token, retain-
ing only the top-K for continued processing. Third, the layers above the gate module process the
selected tokens with token-gated attention, a mechanism that re-weights the attention computation
using the generated importance scores. T OKEN G ATE reduces prefill compute and memory because
pruned tokens are never forwarded through the post-gate layers and these layers never generate KV
cache entries.
Token pruning uses a non-differentiable top-K operator, which presents a challenge for end-to-end
learning. We introduce token-gated attention to overcome this issue. Our method takes inspiration
from Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022), which achieve sparsity
over activated model parameters by gating expert sub-networks. We use a similar form, but in-
stead weight attention logits to achieve sparsity over processed tokens. Using this technique, we
demonstrate that we can adapt existing trained models with cost similar to standard adaptation tech-
niques. For instance, we can fine-tune existing models with T OKEN G ATE using simple next-token-
prediction loss, with no auxiliary loss and total train time similar to supervised fine-tuning on the
base model. The resulting T OKEN G ATE model matches or exceeds accuracy over the trained base
model, while significantly reducing prefill latency and memory.
We evaluate T OKEN G ATE on diverse tasks, including code completion, multi-hop QA, multi-doc
summarization, medical extraction, and needle-in-a-haystack, using both traditional transformer
models and a recent hybrid attention one. Overall, we show the following findings (1) T OKEN -
G ATE reduces TTFT and peak prefill memory by 1.4-11.3× and 1.5-3.4×, respectively, at no accu-
racy degradation compared to the finetuned model baseline with full-context, and outperforms all
training-free token pruning methods, by up to 6.4× faster prefill (TTFT) and 2× lower peak prefill
memory relative to the next-best baseline, (2) T OKEN G ATE natively extends existing recent hybrid-
attention architectures, like Qwen3.5-2B (Qwen Team, 2026), where it achieves 3.8× lower TTFT
over the full-context baseline at no accuracy degradation, and 2.1× lower TTFT than the next best-


                                                                   2
 performing token-pruning method at fixed accuracy. (3) Training models is efficient with T OKEN -
G ATE, incurring minimal overhead compared to standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques,
like LoRA (Hu et al., 2021).
Overall, we summarize our contributions as follows:

• We introduce T OKEN G ATE, a small, drop-in component that extends existing trained models to
  enable end-to-end learnable token pruning for fast and memory-efficient prefill.
• We propose token-gated attention, a mechanism for training models end-to-end despite the gate
  module’s non-differentiable top-K operator.
• Our systematic evaluation finds that T OKEN G ATE reduces TTFT and peak prefill memory by up
  to 6.4× and 2×, respectively, compared to the next best-performing baselines, T OKEN G ATE na-
  tively extends transformer-based models, including recent hybrid-attention architectures. Further,
  training is efficient, with total train time comparable to standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning
  techniques.

2    R ELATED W ORKS
Training-free Token Pruning. One body of prior work optimizes prefill using training-free token-
pruning methods (e.g., FastKV, SlimInfer, DASH, and GemFilter) (Jo et al., 2025; Long et al., 2025;
3.1      P ROBLEM S ETTING

We consider an LLM input prompt x = [xR , xD ], where xR = (x1 , . . . , xr ) is a request instruction
or question and xD = (xr+1 , . . . , xN ) are the “documents” needed to respond to it, such as research
articles, code repositories, medical records, legal documents, or financial filings. In practice, xD
may be supplied by the user or retrieved by a system or an agent given xR . As an example, a user
uploads a document study as a PDF to an AI assistant and asks “what are the side effects reported
in this study?” (Google, 2023; OpenAI, 2025a; Anthropic, 2024; Google, 2025; Microsoft, 2025;
Adobe, 2025; Perplexity AI, 2025; ChatPDF, 2025). Here, xR corresponds to the user’s question,
and xD corresponds to the attached document, which can be thousands to hundreds of thousands of
tokens. Figure 2 shows two such input prompts from our datasets.
In this setting, the documents are provided only at request time, so its KV cache cannot be precom-
puted. Our goal is two-fold: we aim to maximize quality, measured by task accuracy, and minimize
cost, both prefill time-to-first-token (TTFT), which is the latency users experience before seeing any
response, and prefill memory footprint, which limits throughput and concurrent user requests.

T OKEN G ATE is a drop-in neural network component, which places a gate module within a specified
transformer layer1 , L, to score and prune tokens, as shown in Figure 1. In this section, we describe
how T OKEN G ATE enables trainable token pruning using two key components, the gate module
(Section 4.1) and token-gated attention (Section 4.2). We will then overview an end-to-end training
recipe for adapting existing models (Section 4.3).
Overall, the full T OKEN G ATE forward pass with gating at layer L decomposes into three phases.
First, tokens pass through layers below the gate module, using a standard forward pass. Second,
the gate module processes all tokens, producing a score for each, and selecting a subset to prune.
Third, the model performs a pruned forward, processing only selected tokens in layers above the
gate module, using token-gated attention, which re-weights attention scores using the importance
scores. T OKEN G ATE reduces both the compute and memory footprint during prefill by preventing
model layers after the gate module from processing pruned tokens or generating KV-cache entries
for them.

The gate module’s top-K selector introduces a non-differentiability, creating a challenge for end-

Despite T OKEN G ATE’s non-differentiable top-K selection (Eq. 4), the task loss is a differentiable
function of the scoring network, almost everywhere. This is due to token-gated attention, which
injects the top-K gate values into the attention logits at each layer above the token gate. When
we choose K > 1, the gate value gj has non-zero derivatives with respect to the scoring network
weights. This mirrors how the router is trained in MoE through its top-K expert selection: the
router’s value multiplies the output of each selected expert, just as our gate value multiplies the
attention score of each selected token (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022). Intuitively, a token
whose additional attention mass lowers the task loss receives a larger score. A token that distracts
receives a smaller one, allowing the scoring network to learn token importance. This mechanism
allows T OKEN G ATE to be trained end-to-end jointly with the model backbone simply using standard
task losses.

                                         1    Introduction
                                         Safety classiﬁers, commonly called guardrails, are trained and reported like any other classiﬁer. A
                                         paper states a macro-F1 on a held-out split, a set of catch rates on public benchmarks such as Harm-
                                         Bench [17], AdvBench [37], JailbreakBench [2] or StrongREJECT [30], an over-refusal number on
                                         OR-Bench [4] or XSTest [27], and the reader is invited to compare that row against another system’s
                                         row.
                                         This reporting convention contains a silent assumption: that the label unsafe names a property of the
                                         prompt, so that two systems scored on the same prompts are being compared on the same question.
                                         In deployment that assumption is visibly false. “Reproduce the lyrics of this song” is a policy
                                         violation for a content platform and an ordinary request for a drafting assistant. “Tell me a dirty
                                         joke” is blocked by a moderation product and answered by a coding assistant. Neither is a fact about

                                         40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: TAE (Trust-AI-Eval): Can We
                                         Trust AI Evaluation?.
 the string. Each is a decision, made once, by whoever wrote the labelling policy, and then absorbed
by every model trained on those labels.
Most work cannot separate the two, because a project has one labelling policy and therefore one
model family. We separated them by accident. Building a guardrail against a proprietary 24-pillar
safety taxonomy for an on-device assistant, we labelled the same prompt pool twice, a month apart,
with two pipelines judged comparably accurate at the time. They disagreed on one prompt in six, and
the disagreements were not noise: they were systematic, and traced to a difference in the question
the pipeline was answering. Pipeline A asked would a thoughtful moderator block this? Pipeline B
asked is this a request for harmful content? We then trained ten arms (mixing, re-weighting, anchor-
ing, distilling and head-calibrating across the two label families) at two model scales, and evaluated
all twenty models identically on ﬁfteen public safety benchmarks (33,137 prompts).
That grid is a measuring instrument for the evaluation protocols themselves. Our contributions are
diagnostic rather than methodological:

      1. The training corpus contains the benchmark suite (§3). We measure the overlap be-
         tween every benchmark and every pool the grid trained or validated on. It is severe and
         structured: 88% of JailbreakBench-benign and 82% of OR-Bench-hard, against 0% of OR-
         Bench-toxic and 2% of AdvBench. The worst hit are the over-refusal benchmarks, because
         the training class they resemble was built by harvesting them. Everything below is decon-
         taminated.
      2. Benchmarks differ enormously in how much of their score the label deﬁnition decides
         (§4). With architecture and optimiser ﬁxed, changing where the two label families enter
         training moves HarmBench-copyright across its entire range (0.99 of 1.0) and WildGuard-
         benign hardly at all (0.043). But a deﬁnition-unstable benchmark is also seed-unstable,
         and separating the two needs a seed ﬂoor almost nobody reports; we measure one from this
         codebase and show it leaves the middle of that ordering uninterpretable.
      3. A score can be moved across its full range at 0.03% of the parameters (§5). The policy
         is carried by whichever supervision signal is last (head calibration labels, or a distilled
         student’s teacher), not by the training mixture: the arms whose last signal is policy A
         occupy one extreme of HarmBench-copyright and of OR-Bench-hard at both scales (p =
         0.005, 0.14 at worst), while an arm whose hard labels are entirely policy A (40,327 of
         40,327 rows), fully ﬁne-tuned, reaches only 17.3 of 100 on HarmBench-copyright. The
         move leaves no trace in a data card.
      4. Validation accuracy measures policy agreement, not capability (§7). One policy-A-
         labelled split grades all twenty arms and ranks them by policy (ρ = +0.74) rather than by
         detection (ρ = +0.34). It is itself 69.3% inside the policy-A training ﬁle, an overlap we
         found only by running §3’s audit on our own validation data.

None of this says the benchmarks are bad or that the models are bad. It says that a substantial and
unreported fraction of what a guardrail evaluation reports is an answer to “whose policy did you
train on?”, a question the protocol never asks and the paper never states. §8 proposes the minimum
that would ﬁx it.

            occupied = {filename_identity(p.name) for p in self.directory(value).iterdir()}
            occupied.update(r[0] for r in self.db.execute(
                "SELECT normalized_filename FROM run_files WHERE run_date=?", (day,)))
            name = pdf_filename(title)
            counter = 0
            tag = hashlib.sha256(key.encode()).hexdigest()[:10]
            while filename_identity(name) in occupied:
                counter += 1
                suffix = f" [{tag}]" if counter == 1 else f" [{tag}-{counter}]"
                name = pdf_filename(title, suffix)
            self.db.execute("INSERT INTO run_files VALUES (?,?,?,?)",
                            (day, key, name, filename_identity(name)))
            self.db.commit()
            return name
        except Exception:
            self.db.rollback()
            raise

    def entries(self, value):
        rows = self.db.execute(
            "SELECT m.paper_key,m.observation,f.filename FROM membership m "
            "LEFT JOIN run_files f ON f.run_date=m.run_date AND f.paper_key=m.paper_key "
            "WHERE m.run_date=? AND m.role='recent' ORDER BY m.rowid",
            (self.day(value).isoformat(),)).fetchall()
        return [{"key": r["paper_key"], "title": json.loads(r["observation"])["title"],
                 "metadata": json.loads(r["observation"]), "pdf": r["filename"]} for r in rows]

    def ingest(self, value, records, role="recent"):
        if role != "recent":
            raise ValueError("Only selected recent-attention papers are collected")
        folder = self.prepare(value)
        result = []
        for record in records:
            key, p = self.resolve(record)
            with self.db:
                self.db.execute("INSERT OR REPLACE INTO membership VALUES (?,?,?,?)",
                                (self.day(value).isoformat(), key, role, json.dumps(p, ensure_ascii=False)))
                self.db.execute("DELETE FROM exclusions WHERE run_date=? AND paper_key=? AND role=?",
                                (self.day(value).isoformat(), key, role))
            filename = self.allocate_filename(value, key, p["title"])
            cache = self.state / "papers" / key
            cache.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            write_json(cache / "metadata.json", p)
            outcome = {"key": key, "pdf": str(folder / filename), "filename": filename,
                       "text": str(cache / "original.txt")}
            try:
                original = cache / "original.pdf"
                pdf = self.artifact(key, "pdf")
                if pdf:
                    materialize(pdf, original)
                    outcome["download"] = "reused"
                else:
                    download_pdf(p["pdf_url"], original)
                    outcome["download"] = "downloaded"
                self.register(key, "pdf", original)
                checksum = digest(original)
                extraction = cache / "extraction.json"
                text_path = cache / "original.txt"
                if (not text_path.exists() or not extraction.exists()
                        or read_json(extraction).get("pdf_sha256") != checksum):
                    subprocess.run(["pdftotext", "-layout", str(original), str(text_path)],
                                   check=True, capture_output=True, timeout=60)
                    write_json(extraction, {"pdf_sha256": checksum, "extracted_at": now()})
                materialize(original, folder / filename)
            except (OSError, ValueError, subprocess.SubprocessError) as exc:
                outcome["error"] = str(exc)
            write_json(self.work(value) / "ingest" / f"{key}.json", outcome)
            result.append(outcome)
        return result

    def exclude(self, value, key, role, reason):
        """Withdraw a selection, keeping its cache and any previous visible copy."""
        if role != "recent" or not reason.strip():
            raise ValueError("Exclude requires a recent selection and a reason")
        day = self.day(value).isoformat()
        assigned = self.db.execute(
            "SELECT filename FROM run_files WHERE run_date=? AND paper_key=?", (day, key)).fetchone()
        if assigned:
            source = self.directory(value) / assigned[0]
            if source.exists():
                excluded = self.run_state(value) / "excluded"
                excluded.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
                destination = excluded / f"{key}-{datetime.now(timezone.utc):%H%M%S%f}.pdf"
                source.rename(destination)
        with self.db:
            self.db.execute("INSERT OR REPLACE INTO exclusions VALUES (?,?,?,?)", (day, key, role, reason))
            self.db.execute("DELETE FROM membership WHERE run_date=? AND paper_key=? AND role=?", (day, key, role))

    def render_report(self, value, records):
        if not isinstance(records, list):
            raise ValueError("Briefs must be a JSON array")
        entries = {p["key"]: p for p in self.entries(value)}
        keys = [r.get("key") for r in records]
        if len(keys) != len(set(keys)) or set(keys) != set(entries):
            raise ValueError("Provide exactly one brief per included paper")
        blocks, receipt = [], []
        for record in records:
            entry = entries[record["key"]]
            values = {}
            for name in ("why_en", "how_en", "why_zh", "how_zh"):
                value_text = record.get(name)
                if not isinstance(value_text, str) or not value_text.strip():
                    raise ValueError(f"{record['key']}: missing {name}")
                values[name] = value_text.strip()
                if "\n" in values[name] or "\r" in values[name]:
                    raise ValueError(f"{record['key']}: {name} must be a single concise paragraph")
            english_words = len((values["why_en"] + " " + values["how_en"]).split())
            if english_words > MAX_ENGLISH_WORDS:
                raise ValueError(f"{record['key']}: WHY + HOW has {english_words} English words; maximum 100")
                raise ValueError(f"{record['key']}: WHY + HOW has {english_words} English words; maximum 100")
            if not all(re.search(r"[A-Za-z]", values[n]) for n in ("why_en", "how_en")):
                raise ValueError("English WHY and HOW are required")
            if not all(re.search(r"[\u3400-\u9fff]", values[n]) for n in ("why_zh", "how_zh")):
                raise ValueError("Chinese WHY and HOW are required")
            uploaded = record.get("published_at", "")
            if date.fromisoformat(uploaded).isoformat() != uploaded:
                raise ValueError("Use an ISO YYYY-MM-DD first-upload date")
            if uploaded != entry["metadata"].get("published_at", "")[:10]:
                raise ValueError(f"{record['key']}: upload date disagrees with registered metadata")
            if not entry["pdf"]:
                raise ValueError(f"{record['key']}: PDF filename is missing")
            pdf = self.directory(value) / entry["pdf"]
            artifact = self.artifact(record["key"], "pdf")
            if not artifact or not pdf.is_file() or pdf.is_symlink() or digest(pdf) != digest(artifact):
                raise ValueError(f"{record['key']}: missing or corrupted original PDF")
            title = entry["title"].replace("\\", "\\\\").replace("[", "\\[").replace("]", "\\]")
            blocks.append(
                f"## [{title}]({quote(entry['pdf'])})\n\n"
                f"上传日期：{uploaded}\n\n"
                f"**WHY (EN):** {values['why_en']}\n\n"
                f"**HOW (EN):** {values['how_en']}\n\n"
                f"**WHY（中文）：** {values['why_zh']}\n\n"
                f"**HOW（中文）：** {values['how_zh']}\n")
            receipt.append({"key": record["key"], "pdf": entry["pdf"],
                            "pdf_sha256": digest(pdf), "published_at": uploaded,
                            "english_words": english_words})
        return ("\n".join(blocks) if blocks else "本周没有符合筛选条件的论文。\n"), receipt

    def report(self, value, records):
        content, entries = self.render_report(value, records)
        path = self.directory(value) / "README.md"
        with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(mode="w", encoding="utf-8", dir=path.parent,
                                         delete=False, suffix=".tmp") as output:
            output.write(content)
            temporary = output.name
        os.replace(temporary, path)
        write_json(self.work(value) / "briefs.json", records)
        write_json(self.run_state(value) / "report.json", {
            "generated_at": now(), "sha256": digest(path), "papers": entries})
        return {"report": str(path), "papers": len(entries),
                "max_english_words": max((r["english_words"] for r in entries), default=0)}

    def finalize(self, value):
        day = self.day(value).isoformat()
        folder, work, run_state = self.directory(value), self.work(value), self.run_state(value)
        problems, entries = [], self.entries(value)
        exclusions = [dict(r) for r in self.db.execute(
            "SELECT paper_key,role,reason FROM exclusions WHERE run_date=?", (day,))]
        for entry in entries:
            pdf = folder / entry["pdf"] if entry["pdf"] else None
            original = self.artifact(entry["key"], "pdf")
            if (not original or not pdf or not pdf.is_file() or pdf.is_symlink()
                    or digest(original) != digest(pdf)):
                problems.append(f"{entry['key']}: missing or corrupted original PDF")
            else:
                entry["pdf_sha256"] = digest(pdf)
        report_path = folder / "README.md"
        report_receipt = run_state / "report.json"
        briefs_path = work / "briefs.json"
        if not report_path.is_file() or not report_receipt.is_file() or not briefs_path.is_file():
            problems.append("Weekly report or its validation receipt is missing")
        else:
            try:
                expected, details = self.render_report(value, read_json(briefs_path))
                recorded = read_json(report_receipt)
                if report_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8") != expected or digest(report_path) != recorded["sha256"]:
                    problems.append("Weekly report differs from the validated concise format")
                if details != recorded["papers"]:
                    problems.append("Weekly report metadata or original PDF changed; review and regenerate")
            except (ValueError, TypeError, KeyError, OSError) as exc:
                problems.append(f"Invalid weekly brief: {exc}")
        allowed = {e["pdf"] for e in entries} | {"README.md"}
        if folder.exists():
            unexpected = sorted(p.name for p in folder.iterdir() if p.name not in allowed)
            if unexpected:
                problems.append("Unexpected files in weekly directory: " + ", ".join(unexpected))
        discovery_path = work / "discovery.json"
        discovery = read_json(discovery_path) if discovery_path.exists() else {}
        if not discovery.get("healthy_sources"):
            problems.append("No successful discovery source; cannot claim an empty week")

Learning from
                     Fleet Experience:
                     A Collective Learning Paradigm
arXiv:2610.25736v1 [cs.RO] 19 Oct 2026




                     for Robots
                          The fleet becomes a source of experience
                          https://cel-robot-learning.github.io




Tsinghua University / AgiBot / Infinigence AI
                                               Abstract
Experience generated during deployment offers an opportunity for robots to improve policy reliability
through learning from their own executions. However, learning through human corrections requires
teleoperators to monitor execution and intervene when policies fail, a demand that is difficult to meet
as robot fleets grow. We introduce collective experience learning (CEL), a learning paradigm in which
deployed robots share their execution experience to improve a common policy. We realize CEL
through failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning (FERT), which uses failure contexts from robot
executions to retrieve relevant trajectory segments from the fleet's shared successful experience and
uses their actions as supervision for policy updates, without collecting additional expert
demonstrations or corrective actions. A fault-tolerant asynchronous training system (FATS)
coordinates experience collection, policy optimization and policy distribution despite local
interruptions within the robot fleet. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, the resulting policies
achieve success rates of 93.3-99.2%, evaluated over 120 trials per task on robots excluded from

Evaluation also remains limited. Many benchmarks primarily test whether an agent can recall or
answer questions over a static past history, rather than whether experience accumulated during
deployment improves subsequent actions under interference and drift [29, 75, 125]. Moreover, as
memory stores grow, unmanaged external memory suffers from retrieval noise, memory pollution,
and negative transfer when task distributions shift [15, 153].
To bridge this gap, we propose the framework of Memory-Centric Continual Learning (MCCL).
We argue that addressing the stability–plasticity dilemma does not strictly require continuous
gradient updates to foundation model weights. Instead, memory itself can serve as an evolving
learning infrastructure through which an agent incorporates feedback, refines strategies, and resolves
knowledge conflicts during deployment, while keeping the base model intact. In this framework,
continual learning operates as a coupled dynamical system. An inner memory-state loop updates
stored knowledge from sequential deployment experience, while an outer policy-adaptation loop
refines memory management policies based on task performance. By connecting task outcomes back
to memory management, MCCL provides a principled route toward Recursive Self-Improvement
(RSI), where agents not only accumulate experience but also improve how that experience is
organized and used. We summarize our core contributions as follows.

     1. A unified taxonomy of memory architecture. We clarify existing classifications through a
        three-axis taxonomy: where experience persists (substrates: contextual, activation, external
        addressable, and adaptive parametric), what form it takes (assets: episodic, semantic, and
        procedural), and how operations are managed (policies: prescribed, deliberative, and
        learned). This separates physical storage from cognitive representation and operational
        control (Section 2).
     2. The memory lifecycle as an engine for continual learning. We formalize memory dynamics
        across five core stages: selective formation, structural consolidation, reactivation and uti-
        lization, knowledge revision and selective forgetting, and feedback-driven policy evolution.
        This formulation explains how raw interactions turn into generalizable knowledge while
        mitigating memory pollution and drift (Section 3).
     3. A behavioral evaluation framework. We distinguish retrieval-level checks from genuine
        continual learning outcomes. We introduce a four-gate retention cascade (preservation,
        access, utilization, and effect) to diagnose failure points, use matched stateful-versus-reset
        comparisons (Δ𝑃𝑡 ) to isolate the effect of accumulated memory, and establish evaluation

learning infrastructure, focusing on whether an agent can continually learn over time rather than
simply retrieve past records. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents
the taxonomy across substrates, assets, and policies. Section 3 details the memory lifecycle as a
continual learning engine. Section 4 formalizes the evaluation framework and memory scaling
laws. Section 5 analyzes applications across digital and physical domains. Section 6 discusses open
challenges in credit assignment, parametric synergy, and trustworthy memory governance. Section 7

4.1.1    Retention: Learning Must Survive Delay and Interference

Section 3.3 distinguishes preservation, access, utilization, and behavioral effect in the memory
lifecycle. Retention evaluation uses the same cascade, but changes the object of measurement from
a stored trace to a capability margin. After delay and subsequent experience, the agent should
still outperform a matched agent deprived of that experience on the same probe. An entry can
remain in a store, or a latent state can remain decodable, while its contribution to later decisions
has vanished. Conversely, a useful procedure may persist without the originating episode. Trace
survival is therefore diagnostic; behavioral persistence is the learning claim.
The four gates yield a testable weakest-gate hypothesis, positing that behavioral retention is bottle-
necked by the least reliable step and that improving an earlier gate does not necessarily raise the
final outcome. Increasing capacity can raise preservation while lowering access through denser
retrieval competition. “The system remembers 𝑥 ” concerns preservation and access; “the system
retained learning from 𝑥 ” additionally requires utilization and effect. With the base model fixed,
continual insertion and eviction in an external store can reduce performance on earlier tasks [148],
and repeated extraction and injection of experience can turn a single-round gain into progressive
collapse [15]. These failures are not confined to catastrophic forgetting in weights, as stored content
can survive while remaining unaccessed, unused, or ineffective.
Time and intervening experience are not interchangeable. A retention protocol should first measure
the immediate gain Δ𝑖0 on capability 𝑖 relative to a memoryless or reset condition, then remeasure
after delay 𝑑 and interference load 𝑚. The normalized retained gain Δ𝑖 ( 𝑑 , 𝑚)/Δ𝑖0 , reported only when
Δ𝑖0 > 0, distinguishes failure to retain from failure to learn. Delay should be specified in wall-clock
time, turns, or token distance; interference should report the number, semantic overlap, and conflict
relation of intervening updates. Substrate-specific traces then localize the broken gate, identifying
deletion, eviction, and rank competition in external memory, or overwriting, state drift, and readout
mismatch in activation and parametric memory (Section 2.1). These outcomes are the quantities
against which capacity, interference, and cost are traded in Section 4.3.


4.1.2    Adaptation: Learning Must Remain Revisable under Change

When facts, preferences, tools, or rules change, retention without revision becomes a source of error.
Section 3.4 already treats conflict resolution, persistent update, and selective forgetting as lifecycle
operations. Evaluation asks a more targeted question, examining whether behavior faithfully
follows a valid update after an environment change without indiscriminate damage to still-useful
capabilities. The relevant evaluation chain is temporal rather than a single write (detection, revision,
recovery, and preservation), which should be quantified via detection delay, steps to recovery, stale-
error duration, and collateral degradation on unchanged probes. Better recall does not automatically
yield more preference-aligned behavior [134], and summary memories can retain factual detail while
losing the preference signal needed after an environmental shift [108].

Component diagnostics should follow the substrate. For external stores, the question is whether
the current record supersedes the stale one and whether retrieval ranks it above obsolete evidence.
Exposed maintenance operations establish that updates are possible, but conversational QA after a
long history does not demonstrate recovery under controlled drift [19]. For parametric and latent
memories, injection accuracy and sequential fact updates are retention and write diagnostics, not
evidence that an acting agent detected an unannounced change or resumed correct tool use [24, 117].
Evaluated models can verbalize that a fact has changed yet fail to propagate that judgment to
the final prediction [107]. A credible adaptation claim therefore requires matched pre-change and
post-change probes, together with simultaneous reporting of recovery and selective preservation.

4.1.3    Transfer: Learning Must Extend beyond Remembered Episodes
Section 2 classifies reusable experience as episodic, semantic, or procedural assets. Transfer evalua-
tion asks whether those assets support later behavior beyond storing an answer. Three increasingly
demanding cases should be separated: replaying the same or a near-duplicate episode, solving an
unseen variant from the same task family, and applying shared structure to a distinct target task.
Source and target partitions must exclude duplicate instances and target answers, document the
shared structure, such as a workflow, causal rule, tool convention, or subskill, while keeping the base
model, tools, context budget, and compute matched. Otherwise nearest-neighbour reproduction
and extra context can be mistaken for learned transfer.
Abstraction directly supports reuse, as demonstrated by the successful transfer of insights, work-
flows, and executable skills across related tasks and environments [111, 121, 163]. The same evidence
shows why mean target accuracy is insufficient. Raw trajectory memory can produce negative
forward transfer where abstract insights do not, with harm concentrated on cases that a no-memory
agent could not already solve [47]. Dedicated memory and skill-maintenance methods are only selec-
tively helpful and can be matched or outperformed by ordinary in-context accumulation [6, 40, 166].
Transfer should therefore be reported as zero-shot target gain or forward transfer, interactions or
tokens to a target threshold, and explicit negative-transfer rates [71, 91]. For external memory,
analysis should identify whether the retrieved asset is a case, rule, workflow, or skill, and whether
success depends on answer overlap. For neural memory, it should test whether updated latent or
parametric state improves a held-out target without degrading unrelated tasks.

4.2     How to Measure: Protocols for Experience, Controls, and Time

4.2.1    Benchmarks Must Contain Learnable Experience
A parallel distinction applies to benchmark design. The presence of “history” does not imply the
presence of learnable experience. Many suites pre-supply dialogue logs, profiles, or knowledge bases
and then test whether related questions can be answered after the history is given [29, 75, 125, 167].
Such protocols diagnose long-horizon access. They usually cannot decide whether a new capability
was formed during evaluation.
Evidence strength rises with the experience that the protocol actually exposes (Table 2). Fixed history
supports “remember and use.” Continual writing of state supports “internal state accumulates.”
Feedback that improves later behavior, under the matched and sequential controls below, approaches
continual learning. Procedural streams ask whether success and failure trajectories improve later
workflows [165]; semantic and personalization streams ask whether facts and preferences persist
and can be revised [75, 101, 125]; dynamic-rule streams ask whether invalidated experience is
corrected in time [6, 48]. A benchmark may excel on one stream while remaining silent on the others.
Externally grounded outcomes and user corrections also support stronger learning claims than
self-generated reflections, which can be stored and later retrieved as if they were facts [87, 95].

4.2.2    Matched Comparisons Reveal What Memory Contributes
Even when performance rises across a task sequence, the gain cannot be attributed to memory until
alternative explanations are removed. The backbone, a longer context, static retrieval, or additional
inference can produce similar effects. Figure 6 isolates accumulated experience by comparing a

        "title": "Learning from Fleet Experience: A Collective Learning Paradigm for Robots",
        "abstract": "Experience generated during deployment offers an opportunity for robots to improve policy reliability through learning from their own executions. However, learning through human corrections requires teleoperators to monitor execution and intervene when policies fail, a demand that is difficult to meet as robot fleets grow. We introduce collective experience learning (CEL), a learning paradigm in which deployed robots share their execution experience to improve a common policy. We realize CEL through failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning (FERT), which uses failure contexts from robot executions to retrieve relevant trajectory segments from the fleet's shared successful experience and uses their actions as supervision for policy updates, without collecting additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions. A fault-tolerant asynchronous training system (FATS) coordinates experience collection, policy optimization and policy distribution despite local interruptions within the robot fleet. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, the resulting policies achieve success rates of 93.3-99.2%, evaluated over 120 trials per task on robots excluded from training data collection. With collection time per robot held fixed, larger fleets provide more experience and FERT generally achieves higher success rates across the evaluated sizes. On multi-stage phone packaging, learning with 96 robots increases success from 79.2% to 98.3%. These results support collective experience as a practical basis for scalable robot learning and a path towards improving policy reliability during deployment without collecting additional expert corrective actions.",

        "abstract": "This paper presents the design, implementation, and evaluation of the PyTorch\ndistributed data parallel module. Data parallelism has emerged as a popular solution for\ndistributed training thanks to its straightforward principle and broad\napplicability. In general, the technique of distributed data parallelism\nreplicates the model on every computational resource to generate gradients\nindependently and then communicates those gradients at each iteration to keep\nmodel replicas consistent. Despite the conceptual simplicity of the technique,\nthe subtle dependencies between computation and communication make it\nnon-trivial to optimize the distributed training efficiency. As of v1.5,\nPyTorch natively provides several techniques to accelerate distributed data\nparallel, including bucketing gradients, overlapping computation with\ncommunication, and skipping gradient synchronization.       "metadata": {
        "title": "Scaling Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Brain Encoding",
        "abstract": "Brain encoding models aim to predict neural responses to stimuli. The most widely used approach fits readouts from frozen pretrained backbones. Using neural data to train large models from scratch or fully fine-tune them after task-pretraining has proven difficult because neural data is costly and limited. We show that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables us to effectively adapt very large pretrained backbones for brain encoding with a small number of trainable parameters. To make it computationally practical, we exploit the backbone's causal structure to predict multiple timepoints in a single pass instead of using sliding windows, significantly reducing feature-extraction cost. This enables efficient fine-tuning of multimodal backbones with up to 104B parameters, the largest model adapted for brain encoding to our knowledge. Trained with a low-rank adapter (LoRA) and a lightweight readout, our approach consistently improves brain encoding performance across nine diverse multimodal backbones. On the same Qwen3-Omni backbone as the prior state-of-the-art (SoTA), our method BrainLoRA achieves the best published performance on the Algonauts 2025 Challenge. We also show the adapted multimodal backbones remain interpretable: modality attribution recovers the canonical sensory topography that prior work often obtains by construction from separate unimodal encoders, and neural adaptation increases the contribution of audio inputs and cross-modal mixing within the backbone. To scale out the number of adapted models, we develop a multi-LoRA kernel that accelerates joint training of multiple LoRAs on a shared backbone. This enables an ensemble of 200+ adapted models that ranks first on the public Algonauts post-challenge leaderboard at the time of writing. Together, our results highlight PEFT as an efficient and powerful paradigm for brain encoding.",

      "key": "arxiv-2610.29357",
      "title": "Memory-Centric Continual Learning for AI Agents",
      "metadata": {
        "title": "Memory-Centric Continual Learning for AI Agents",
        "abstract": "Autonomous agents powered by foundation models can reason, plan, and use tools, but their fixed weights and context limits hinder sustained learning from experience over long-term deployment. While external memory systems attempt to bridge this gap, they mostly act as passive retrieval caches, evaluated primarily by whether they can recall stored facts or past interactions. Whether memory can drive genuine continual learning remains an open question. In this paper, we introduce Memory-Centric Continual Learning (MCCL), arguing that memory should be judged by whether it improves future actions, not merely what it retrieves. MCCL has three main parts. First, a three-axis taxonomy organizes memory by where state is stored (substrates), what form it takes (assets), and how it is managed (policies). This defines a two-loop lifecycle that updates memory state in an inner loop while refining management policies in an outer loop based on task feedback. Second, an evaluation protocol measures retention under interference, adaptation to change, and task transfer to isolate genuine behavioral gains from simple context expansion. Third, a memory scaling framework models how agent performance scales with experience, storage capacity, and compute budgets across non-parametric and parametric memory. Together, these components reframe agent memory from passive lookup to continuous learning, offering a principled route toward self-improving autonomous agents.",

        "title": "Ultralytics YOLO26: Unified Real-Time End-to-End Vision Models",
        "abstract": "Real-time vision demands models that are accurate, efficient, and simple to deploy across diverse hardware. The YOLO family has become widely deployed for this reason, yet most YOLO detectors still rely on non-maximum suppression at inference, carry heavy detection heads due to Distribution Focal Loss, require long training schedules, and can leave the smallest objects without positive label assignments. We present Ultralytics YOLO26, a unified real-time vision model family that addresses these limitations through coordinated architecture and training advances. YOLO26 uses a dual-head design for native NMS-free end-to-end inference and removes DFL entirely, yielding a lighter head with unconstrained regression range. Its training pipeline combines MuSGD, a hybrid Muon-SGD optimizer adapted from large language model training; Progressive Loss, which shifts supervision toward the inference-time head; and STAL, a label assignment strategy that guarantees positive coverage for small objects. Beyond detection, YOLO26 introduces task-specific head and loss designs for instance segmentation, pose estimation, and oriented detection, producing consistent gains across tasks and scales. The family spans five scales (n/s/m/l/x) and supports detection, instance segmentation, pose estimation, classification, and oriented detection in a single pipeline, with an open-vocabulary extension, YOLOE-26, for text-, visual-, and prompt-free inference. Across all scales, YOLO26 achieves 40.9-57.5 mAP on COCO at 1.7-11.8 ms T4 TensorRT latency, advancing the accuracy-latency Pareto front over prior real-time detectors, while YOLOE-26x reaches 40.6 AP on LVIS minival under text prompting.         "title": "Evaluating Agentic Capabilities Before Post-Training: An End-to-End Approach",
        "abstract": "Agentic capabilities are increasingly important for modern LLMs, yet remain difficult to evaluate during pretraining. Existing approaches typically rely on static trajectory-derived tasks or likelihood-based proxies, which are lightweight but provide limited visibility into how base models behave in interactive environments. We introduce ASAP (Agent Scaffold Adaptation for Pretraining Evaluation), a lightweight framework for eliciting and evaluating agentic behavior from pretrained base models on end-to-end tasks. Rather than converting base models into chat-style agents, ASAP preserves the completion interface and adapts existing agent scaffolds through structured trajectory continuation, short reference prefixes, and minimal recovery mechanisms. Across software-engineering and deep-research benchmarks, ASAP yields discriminative end-to-end performance across base models and pretraining checkpoints. Beyond aggregate scores, ASAP exposes model-generated execution trajectories, enabling analysis of exploration, editing, testing, recovery, and task completion across training stages. These trajectories provide a behavioral view of how agent-relevant capabilities change during pretraining and how execution patterns differ after post-training.         "title": "Deep Fusion Memory: A Chunk-Level Parametric Memory for Large Language Models",
        "abstract": "Large language models need effective ways to acquire and use external knowledge beyond what they retain from pretraining. Continued pretraining risks catastrophic forgetting, while retrieval at inference time can add substantial overhead. External parametric memory avoids online retrieval, but constructing its training data requires extensive offline search, and output-level interpolation provides only shallow fusion. We introduce Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), a parametric memory architecture that reduces this construction workload and incorporates learned memory into intermediate hidden states. A causal memory predictor learns to generate memory from the preceding context, using retrieved chunk embeddings from the corpus as supervision. The predicted memory is shared across tokens within each chunk and fused into their hidden states through gated cross-attention. Memory prediction and fusion are trained end to end with the backbone frozen, and inference requires no explicit retrieval. Compared with existing parametric memory approaches, which often construct token-level memory targets, DFM requires 32times fewer retrieval queries and 2048times fewer retrieved items to construct its training data. Across six QA tasks, DFM performs better over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA, domain adaptation yields average gains of 6.51 and 4.38 points over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively.",

## [Learning from Fleet Experience: A Collective Learning Paradigm for Robots](Learning%20from%20Fleet%20Experience%20-%20A%20Collective%20Learning%20Paradigm%20for%20Robots.pdf)

上传日期：2026-10-19

**WHY (EN):** Robots can improve after deployment, but relying on human corrections for every failure limits fleet-scale learning.

**HOW (EN):** FERT retrieves successful trajectory segments using failure contexts and prioritizes their actions for supervised policy updates; FATS asynchronously coordinates robot experience collection, training, and policy rollout.

**WHY（中文）：** 機器人可從部署經驗中改進，但若每次失敗都仰賴人工糾正，機隊擴展便難以帶動持續學習。

**HOW（中文）：** FERT 以失敗情境檢索成功軌跡片段，優先用其動作監督策略更新；FATS 非同步協調經驗收集、訓練與策略分發。

## [PyTorch Distributed: Experiences on Accelerating Data Parallel Training](PyTorch%20Distributed%20-%20Experiences%20on%20Accelerating%20Data%20Parallel%20Training.pdf)

上传日期：2020-06-28

**WHY (EN):** Data-parallel training wastes time when gradient communication cannot overlap with the backward pass.

**HOW (EN):** PyTorch DDP groups gradients into buckets and uses autograd hooks to launch asynchronous AllReduce when each bucket is ready, overlapping communication with remaining computation.

**WHY（中文）：** 資料平行訓練若梯度通訊無法與反向傳播重疊，便會浪費計算時間。

**HOW（中文）：** PyTorch DDP 將梯度分桶，並由自動微分鉤子在分桶就緒時啟動非同步 AllReduce，讓通訊與後續計算重疊。

## [Scaling Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Brain Encoding](Scaling%20Parameter-Efficient%20Fine-Tuning%20for%20Brain%20Encoding.pdf)

上传日期：2026-10-19

**WHY (EN):** Frozen readouts cannot specialize large backbones, while full fine-tuning is costly when neural data is scarce.

**HOW (EN):** A causal single-pass feature path encodes all time points together; rank-16 LoRA adapters and lightweight readouts adapt the backbone, while a fused multi-LoRA kernel trains many adapters jointly.

**WHY（中文）：** 只訓練讀出層無法使大型骨幹充分特化，而神經資料稀少時，全量微調的成本又很高。

**HOW（中文）：** 因果式單次前向路徑同時編碼各時間點；模型以 rank-16 LoRA 與輕量讀出層適配骨幹，並用融合式 multi-LoRA 核心共同訓練多組適配器。

## [Memory-Centric Continual Learning for AI Agents](Memory-Centric%20Continual%20Learning%20for%20AI%20Agents.pdf)

上传日期：2026-10-21

**WHY (EN):** Agent memory can retain information without preserving useful behavior when tasks change or experiences interfere.

**HOW (EN):** MCCL models continual learning as coupled memory-state and feedback-updated management-policy loops, and specifies stateful-versus-reset tests for behavioral retention, adaptation, and transfer.

**WHY（中文）：** 代理記憶可能留住資訊，卻未必能在任務變動或經驗互相干擾時維持有效行為。

**HOW（中文）：** MCCL 將持續學習描述為記憶狀態迴圈與回饋更新的管理策略迴圈，並提出以保留狀態對照重置狀態來測量保留、適應與遷移。

## [Ultralytics YOLO26: Unified Real-Time End-to-End Vision Models](Ultralytics%20YOLO26%20-%20Unified%20Real-Time%20End-to-End%20Vision%20Models.pdf)

上传日期：2026-06-02

**WHY (EN):** Long training schedules make real-time detector development expensive.

**HOW (EN):** YOLO26 uses MuSGD, which mixes Muon’s orthogonalized momentum updates with momentum SGD for matrix-valued weights while retaining SGD for biases and normalization parameters.

**WHY（中文）：** 即時物件偵測器往往需要漫長訓練，使開發成本偏高。

**HOW（中文）：** YOLO26 採用 MuSGD：對矩陣權重混合 Muon 正交化動量更新與動量 SGD，對偏置與正規化參數則保留 SGD。

**WHY (EN):** Static proxies reveal little about how interactive agent capabilities emerge during language-model pretraining.

**HOW (EN):** ASAP adapts completion-style base models to agent scaffolds using short verified trajectory prefixes and minimal recovery rules, then analyzes step-level behavior across pretraining checkpoints.

**WHY（中文）：** 靜態代理任務難以呈現互動式代理能力如何在語言模型預訓練中形成。

**HOW（中文）：** ASAP 以經核實的短軌跡前綴和精簡復原規則，將補全文本式基礎模型接入代理框架，再比較不同預訓練檢查點的逐步行為。

## [Deep Fusion Memory: A Chunk-Level Parametric Memory for Large Language Models](Deep%20Fusion%20Memory%20-%20A%20Chunk-Level%20Parametric%20Memory%20for%20Large%20Language%20Models.pdf)

上传日期：2026-10-18

**WHY (EN):** Continued pretraining can overwrite prior knowledge, while online retrieval adds cost when language models acquire domain information.

**HOW (EN):** DFM trains chunk-level memory predictors and gated cross-attention modules against retrieval-derived targets while freezing the backbone, fusing predicted memory into decoder states without retrieval at inference.

**WHY（中文）：** 持續預訓練可能覆寫既有知識，而線上檢索會增加語言模型取得領域資訊時的成本。

**HOW（中文）：** DFM 凍結骨幹，以檢索所得目標訓練區塊級記憶預測器與閘控交叉注意力模組，將預測記憶融合進解碼器狀態，推論時無須檢索。

## [Policy Is Not Capability: Some Safety Benchmarks Measure Which Definition of "Unsafe" You Trained On](Policy%20Is%20Not%20Capability%20-%20Some%20Safety%20Benchmarks%20Measure%20Which%20Definition%20of%20-%20Unsafe%20-%20You%20Trained%20On.pdf)

上传日期：2026-10-18

**WHY (EN):** Guardrail benchmark scores can reflect the label policy learned during training rather than detection capability alone.

**HOW (EN):** Across ten training arms, the study varies how two label policies enter supervised training, distillation, and head-only calibration while holding architecture and optimizer family fixed, tracing their effects on evaluation.

**WHY（中文）：** 安全護欄的基準分數可能反映訓練時學到的標註政策，而不只是偵測能力。

**HOW（中文）：** 研究比較十種訓練設定，改變兩種標註政策進入監督訓練、蒸餾與僅訓練輸出頭的方式，並固定架構和最佳化器家族來追蹤評測變化。

## [Answering in the User's Variety: Calibrated Accommodation Pairs for Post-Training](Answering%20in%20the%20User%27s%20Variety%20-%20Calibrated%20Accommodation%20Pairs%20for%20Post-Training.pdf)

上传日期：2026-10-20

**WHY (EN):** Post-training can standardize replies while favoring some dialect features, and output audits miss stage-specific preferences.

**HOW (EN):** Content-matched prompts diagnose SFT, DPO, and RL updates; calibrated accommodation pairs encode DPO preferences that distinguish user-matched feature density from over-accommodation and dialect imposition.

**WHY（中文）：** 後訓練可能使回覆趨於標準化並偏好某些方言特徵，單看輸出難以辨認各階段的偏好。

**HOW（中文）：** 研究以內容相同的提示診斷 SFT、DPO 與 RL 更新；校準式語言調適偏好組則用 DPO 區分貼合使用者特徵密度、過度調適與強加方言。

## [TokenGate: Adapting LLMs for Fast and Memory-Efficient Prefill with Learned Token Pruning](TokenGate%20-%20Adapting%20LLMs%20for%20Fast%20and%20Memory-Efficient%20Prefill%20with%20Learned%20Token%20Pruning.pdf)

**HOW (EN):** A learned gate keeps the top-K tokens at an intermediate layer; token-gated attention carries their importance scores into later layers, enabling end-to-end adaptation of the gate and model.

**WHY（中文）：** 長提示中的每個詞元都經過所有解碼器層，造成預填充計算與 KV 記憶體浪費。

**HOW（中文）：** 學習式閘門在中間層保留 top-K 詞元；詞元閘控注意力將重要性分數帶入後續層，讓閘門與模型可端到端適配。
